# Exercise 3.2 — Loss functions {#sec-loss-functions}


## Overview

 A loss function scores a candidate line against the data; the fitting procedure returns the line with the lowest score. Here you will aim to understand what a loss function is, starting from computing a residual, to a sum of squared residuals, a mean squared error and a
  mean absolute error from a set of predictions.


:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

[**Download the R code from this chapter**](code/day3-02-loss-functions.R){download="day3-02-loss-functions.R"} — every cell below, in page
order, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Positron beside the
page and run it a chunk at a time.

### The data

A loss function needs something to score, so start from the 80 patients and a
line somebody drew by hand.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")

glu
```

### Step 1 — One patient, one residual

A residual is what the model got wrong for one patient:

$$r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$

Take a line nobody fitted — $\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 120 + 0.5 \times
\text{age}$, invented by hand. Add two columns: what that line predicts, and
how far each patient is from it.

```{r}
glu <- glu |>
  mutate(pred_guess  = 120 + 0.5 * age,
         resid_guess = glucose - pred_guess)

glu
```

Now find the patient the line serves worst — the largest residual, in either
direction.

```{r}
glu |> slice_max(abs(resid_guess), n = 1)
```

That patient is 58, their measured glucose is 72, the hand-drawn line predicts
149, and the residual is −77 mg/dL — an error larger than the measurement
itself.

The red segments below are the residuals, one per patient. A loss function is
a rule for turning all 80 of them into a single number.

```{r}
ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 120, slope = 0.5,
              colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = age, yend = pred_guess),
               colour = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)")
```

### Step 2 — From 80 residuals to one number

Residuals are positive and negative, so adding them up cancels most of the
error away. Two repairs are in common use, and they are not the same.

Square each residual, or take its size and ignore the sign:

```{r}
glu <- glu |>
  mutate(squared  = resid_guess^2,
         absolute = abs(resid_guess))

glu |> select(age, glucose, resid_guess, squared, absolute)
```

Then add them up, or average them:

$$\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \left| r_i \right|$$

```{r}
glu |>
  summarise(SSR  = sum(squared),
            MSE  = mean(squared),
            RMSE = sqrt(mean(squared)),
            MAE  = mean(absolute)) |>
  round(2)
```

Four names for four lines of that summary:

| | What it is | On this line |
|---|---|---|
| **SSR** | sum of squared residuals | 90,868 |
| **MSE** | the same, divided by the 80 patients | 1,135.9 |
| **RMSE** | the square root of the MSE, back in mg/dL | 33.7 |
| **MAE** | the average size of an error, in mg/dL | 28.7 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,54,32]"}

Squaring is the L2 loss; taking the absolute value is the L1 loss. Dividing by
the number of patients is what stops the score growing simply because the
dataset is larger. RMSE and MAE are both in mg/dL and the RMSE is the larger of
the two, which is not an accident: squaring weights the worst patients more
heavily, so any summary built from squares sits above the plain average error
whenever the residuals are unequal.

### Task 1 — Score the fitted line against the hand-drawn one

Fit the least-squares line, add its predictions and residuals as two more
columns, and summarise them the same way.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
fit_ols <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

glu <- glu |>
  mutate(pred_ols  = predict(fit_ols),
         resid_ols = ______)

glu |>
  summarise(MSE = mean(resid_ols^2),
            MAE = mean(abs(resid_ols))) |>
  round(2)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
fit_ols <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

glu <- glu |>
  mutate(pred_ols  = predict(fit_ols),
         resid_ols = glucose - pred_ols)

glu |>
  summarise(MSE = mean(resid_ols^2),
            MAE = mean(abs(resid_ols))) |>
  round(2)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
A residual is the measurement minus the prediction, exactly as it was for the
hand-drawn line two steps ago. The columns you need are `glucose` and
`pred_ols`.
:::

The fitted line scores MSE 847.5 against the hand-drawn line's 1,135.9, and MAE
22.3 against 28.7. It wins on both. That is reassuring but not guaranteed: the
fitted line is the best line *for squared error*, and nothing in the procedure
promises it also has the lowest absolute error. Hold that thought.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Task 2 — Contaminate three readings

Three glucose values are recorded three times too large — a plausible unit or
transcription error. Multiply patients 1, 3 and 5 by three, fit the line
again, and compare the two sets of coefficients.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu_bad <- glu |>
  mutate(glucose = if_else(row_number() %in% c(1, 3, 5),
                           glucose * ______, glucose))

fit_bad <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = ______)

rbind(clean        = coef(fit_ols),
      contaminated = coef(fit_bad))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
glu_bad <- glu |>
  mutate(glucose = if_else(row_number() %in% c(1, 3, 5),
                           glucose * 3, glucose))

fit_bad <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu_bad)

rbind(clean        = coef(fit_ols),
      contaminated = coef(fit_bad))
```
:::
:::

Three rows out of eighty — under four per cent of the data — moved the
intercept from 110.3 to 135.3 and turned the slope from +0.289 to −0.136. The
fitted line now says glucose *falls* with age. Nothing warned you; the fit
succeeded, as it always does.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 3 — Which line is better depends on the loss

The obvious reading is that outliers break regression. They do not. They break
*this loss*.

You now have two lines: the clean one and the contaminated one. Score both of
them on the contaminated data, once with squared error and once with absolute
error.

```{r}
b_clean <- coef(fit_ols)
b_bad   <- coef(fit_bad)

glu_bad |>
  mutate(r_clean = glucose - (b_clean[1] + b_clean[2] * age),
         r_bad   = glucose - (b_bad[1]   + b_bad[2]   * age)) |>
  summarise(MSE_clean = mean(r_clean^2),   MSE_bad = mean(r_bad^2),
            MAE_clean = mean(abs(r_clean)), MAE_bad = mean(abs(r_bad))) |>
  round(1)
```

The two losses disagree about which line is better:

| | the clean line | the contaminated line |
|---|---|---|
| scored by **MSE** | 4,964 | **4,812** |
| scored by **MAE** | **32.9** | 36.5 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

By squared error the contaminated line wins, which it must — that is the
quantity the fitting procedure minimised. By absolute error the clean line
wins, even on the contaminated data. Tripling a glucose of 194 to 582
multiplies its contribution to the MSE by roughly the square of how far out it
now is, so the line is dragged towards it; under absolute error that patient
contributes its distance and no more, and three votes out of eighty do not
carry.

So "the best fit line" is not a property of the data. It is a property of the
data *and the loss you chose*, and the choice was made for you by whoever wrote
`lm()`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why squared error anyway
If absolute error is this much more robust, why is every default squared? Two
reasons, and only one of them is about statistics. The squared loss is
differentiable everywhere, which is what lets Exercise 3.4 follow a
gradient and Exercise 3.5 solve for the answer in closed form; absolute error has a
kink at zero and needs a different class of algorithm. And the mean is the
minimiser of squared error while the median minimises absolute error, so the
two losses are answering different questions about the outcome, not the same
question with different robustness. Convenience, then interpretation — in that
order, historically.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A loss takes a line and returns a number. Every line you have scored so far was
handed to you — by a colleague's pen, or by `lm()`. Exercise 3.3 turns that
round: hold the data fixed, let the two parameters vary, and look for the pair
that scores lowest. That is all fitting is.

### The data

A loss function needs something to score, so start from the 80 patients and a
line somebody drew by hand.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

glu = pd.read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")

glu.head()
```

### Step 1 — One patient, one residual

A residual is what the model got wrong for one patient:

$$r_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$

Take a line nobody fitted — $\widehat{\text{glucose}} = 120 + 0.5 \times
\text{age}$, invented by hand. Add two columns: what that line predicts, and
how far each patient is from it.

```{python}
glu["pred_guess"]  = 120 + 0.5 * glu["age"]
glu["resid_guess"] = glu["glucose"] - glu["pred_guess"]

glu.head()
```

Now find the patient the line serves worst — the largest residual, in either
direction.

```{python}
glu.loc[[glu["resid_guess"].abs().idxmax()]]
```

That patient is 58, their measured glucose is 72, the hand-drawn line predicts
149, and the residual is −77 mg/dL — an error larger than the measurement
itself.

The red segments below are the residuals, one per patient. A loss function is
a rule for turning all 80 of them into a single number.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=0.6)
ax.plot(glu["age"], glu["pred_guess"], color="darkorange")
ax.vlines(glu["age"], glu["pred_guess"], glu["glucose"],
          color="red", alpha=0.3)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
plt.show()
```

### Step 2 — From 80 residuals to one number

Residuals are positive and negative, so adding them up cancels most of the
error away. Two repairs are in common use, and they are not the same.

Square each residual, or take its size and ignore the sign:

```{python}
glu["squared"]  = glu["resid_guess"] ** 2
glu["absolute"] = glu["resid_guess"].abs()

glu[["age", "glucose", "resid_guess", "squared", "absolute"]].head()
```

Then add them up, or average them:

$$\text{SSR} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} r_i^2 \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \left| r_i \right|$$

```{python}
pd.Series({"SSR":  glu["squared"].sum(),
           "MSE":  glu["squared"].mean(),
           "RMSE": np.sqrt(glu["squared"].mean()),
           "MAE":  glu["absolute"].mean()}).round(2)
```

Four names for four lines of that summary:

| | What it is | On this line |
|---|---|---|
| **SSR** | sum of squared residuals | 90,868 |
| **MSE** | the same, divided by the 80 patients | 1,135.9 |
| **RMSE** | the square root of the MSE, back in mg/dL | 33.7 |
| **MAE** | the average size of an error, in mg/dL | 28.7 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,54,32]"}

Squaring is the L2 loss; taking the absolute value is the L1 loss. Dividing by
the number of patients is what stops the score growing simply because the
dataset is larger. RMSE and MAE are both in mg/dL and the RMSE is the larger of
the two, which is not an accident: squaring weights the worst patients more
heavily, so any summary built from squares sits above the plain average error
whenever the residuals are unequal.

### Task 1 — Score the fitted line against the hand-drawn one

Fit the least-squares line, add its predictions and residuals as two more
columns, and summarise them the same way.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"]
fit_ols = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

glu["pred_ols"]  = fit_ols.predict(X)
glu["resid_ols"] = ______

pd.Series({"MSE": (glu["resid_ols"] ** 2).mean(),
           "MAE": glu["resid_ols"].abs().mean()}).round(2)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"]
fit_ols = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

glu["pred_ols"]  = fit_ols.predict(X)
glu["resid_ols"] = glu["glucose"] - glu["pred_ols"]

pd.Series({"MSE": (glu["resid_ols"] ** 2).mean(),
           "MAE": glu["resid_ols"].abs().mean()}).round(2)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
A residual is the measurement minus the prediction, exactly as it was for the
hand-drawn line two steps ago. The columns you need are `glucose` and
`pred_ols`.
:::

The fitted line scores MSE 847.5 against the hand-drawn line's 1,135.9, and MAE
22.3 against 28.7. It wins on both. That is reassuring but not guaranteed: the
fitted line is the best line *for squared error*, and nothing in the procedure
promises it also has the lowest absolute error. Hold that thought.

### Task 2 — Contaminate three readings

Three glucose values are recorded three times too large — a plausible unit or
transcription error. Multiply patients 1, 3 and 5 by three, fit the line
again, and compare the two sets of coefficients.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] *= ______

fit_bad = LinearRegression().fit(______[["age"]], ______["glucose"])

pd.DataFrame({"intercept": [fit_ols.intercept_, fit_bad.intercept_],
              "slope":     [fit_ols.coef_[0],   fit_bad.coef_[0]]},
             index=["clean", "contaminated"])
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] *= 3

fit_bad = LinearRegression().fit(glu_bad[["age"]], glu_bad["glucose"])

pd.DataFrame({"intercept": [fit_ols.intercept_, fit_bad.intercept_],
              "slope":     [fit_ols.coef_[0],   fit_bad.coef_[0]]},
             index=["clean", "contaminated"])
```
:::
:::

Three rows out of eighty — under four per cent of the data — moved the
intercept from 110.3 to 135.3 and turned the slope from +0.289 to −0.136. The
fitted line now says glucose *falls* with age. Nothing warned you; the fit
succeeded, as it always does.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 3 — Which line is better depends on the loss

The obvious reading is that outliers break regression. They do not. They break
*this loss*.

You now have two lines: the clean one and the contaminated one. Score both of
them on the contaminated data, once with squared error and once with absolute
error.

```{python}
r_clean = glu_bad["glucose"] - fit_ols.predict(glu_bad[["age"]])
r_bad   = glu_bad["glucose"] - fit_bad.predict(glu_bad[["age"]])

pd.Series({"MSE_clean": (r_clean ** 2).mean(),
           "MSE_bad":   (r_bad ** 2).mean(),
           "MAE_clean": r_clean.abs().mean(),
           "MAE_bad":   r_bad.abs().mean()}).round(1)
```

The two losses disagree about which line is better:

| | the clean line | the contaminated line |
|---|---|---|
| scored by **MSE** | 4,964 | **4,812** |
| scored by **MAE** | **32.9** | 36.5 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

By squared error the contaminated line wins, which it must — that is the
quantity the fitting procedure minimised. By absolute error the clean line
wins, even on the contaminated data. Tripling a glucose of 194 to 582
multiplies its contribution to the MSE by roughly the square of how far out it
now is, so the line is dragged towards it; under absolute error that patient
contributes its distance and no more, and three votes out of eighty do not
carry.

So "the best fit line" is not a property of the data. It is a property of the
data *and the loss you chose*, and the choice was made for you by whoever wrote
`lm()`.

Read the last sentence as `LinearRegression` rather than `lm()`: both minimise
squared error, and neither asks you first.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why squared error anyway
If absolute error is this much more robust, why is every default squared? Two
reasons, and only one of them is about statistics. The squared loss is
differentiable everywhere, which is what lets Exercise 3.4 follow a
gradient and Exercise 3.5 solve for the answer in closed form; absolute error has a
kink at zero and needs a different class of algorithm. And the mean is the
minimiser of squared error while the median minimises absolute error, so the
two losses are answering different questions about the outcome, not the same
question with different robustness. Convenience, then interpretation — in that
order, historically.
:::

## Reflection

1. A colleague reports an RMSE of 29.1 mg/dL and a MAE of 22.3 mg/dL for the
   same model and asks which is the real error. What do you say?
2. You are predicting length of stay so that a bed manager can plan tomorrow's
   discharges. Give one argument for scoring that model with absolute error and
   one for squared error, and say which you would defend to the bed manager.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** Reflection 1: both are real and they measure different things —
RMSE exceeds MAE whenever the residuals are unequal, and the gap between them is
itself a description of the error distribution. Neither is "the" error; the
question to ask back is what decision the number is for. Reflection 2: absolute
error treats a one-day and a ten-day miss proportionally, which matches a
planner counting beds; squared error says a ten-day miss is far worse than ten
one-day misses, which matches a service where a single badly wrong case causes a
cancellation. The defensible answer names the decision, not the formula.

**Expected values** (regenerated data varies in the last digit). Hand-drawn line
$120 + 0.5x$: SSR ≈ 90,000–91,000, MSE ≈ 1130–1140, MAE ≈ 28–29. Fitted line:
MSE ≈ 845–850, MAE ≈ 22–23. Contaminated fit: intercept ≈ 134–136, slope ≈ −0.14
(the sign flip is the point). Scored on the contaminated data, the clean line
beats the contaminated one on MAE (≈ 33 against ≈ 36) and loses on MSE
(≈ 4,960 against ≈ 4,810). The worst-served patient under the hand-drawn line
is aged 58 with a glucose of 72, predicted 149, residual −77. Stretch 2: under
the fitted line the worst-served patient is aged 22 with a glucose of 199, and
that one patient is 10.0% of the total squared error but 4.6% of the total
absolute error — a little over twice the weight, from squaring alone.

**Common failures.** (1) Using row numbers 1, 3, 5 in pandas, where the first
row is 0 — the R tab contaminates patients 1, 3 and 5 and the Python tab rows
0, 2 and 4, which are the same three people. Worth letting them get it wrong,
then asking why the two languages disagreed. (2) Writing the residual the wrong
way round, prediction minus measurement, which leaves the MSE unchanged and the
plot upside down. (3) Reading the contaminated fit as a failure of `lm()` rather
than as `lm()` doing exactly what it was asked to do.

**Plenary.** Put the clean and contaminated coefficient tables side by side and
ask which line a clinician should be shown. Then the two-by-two: scored on the
contaminated data, the clean line loses on MSE and wins on MAE. The sentence to
land is that "best fit" is a property of the data *and the loss*, and that
nobody asked them which loss they wanted.

**Timing.** Nothing here takes a machine any time; the clock goes on the
contamination task and the argument after it. If you are short, set Task 1 as
reading rather than typing — it is the same three verbs as Step 2 — and keep
the full discussion of Task 2.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Where does the squared loss put the line
Contaminate a single patient rather than three, and increase the multiplier
from 1 to 10 in steps, refitting each time. Plot the fitted slope against the
multiplier. The relationship is close to linear, and it has no breakpoint: there
is no size of error at which squared loss decides to ignore a point.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — How much of the loss is one patient
Take the fitted line and work out what share of the total squared error comes
from the single worst-served patient, then the share of the total absolute
error from that same patient. The two shares are not the same number. Say which
is larger, by roughly how much, and what that implies for a model fitted on a
dataset with three bad readings in it.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can compute any of the standard regression losses from
residuals, state what each does with a badly mispredicted patient, and
demonstrate that the best fit line depends on which loss was chosen.

**Cannot:** that you can find the line with the lowest loss. Every line you
scored here was handed to you. Exercise 3.3 treats the loss as a function of the
two parameters and goes looking for the pair that scores lowest.
